subject: Business Models
title: BlackBerry: Keyboard Loyalty
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: BlackBerry: Keyboard Loyalty.

hook.text: BlackBerry owned 50% of the US smartphone market in 2009. By 2016 its share was 0%. The iPhone happened.

buildup.text: BlackBerry's physical keyboard was beloved by enterprise users. Email on the go was its killer feature.

discovery.text: The iPhone replaced the keyboard with a touchscreen. BlackBerry's CEO said consumers wouldn't want to type on glass.

twist.text: BlackBerry could have pivoted to software and security—its strengths. Instead it kept making hardware nobody wanted.

climax.text: BlackBerry confused its product (keyboards) with its value (secure mobile). The value survived; the product didn't.

punchline.text: 50% to 0% in 7 years. BlackBerry loved its keyboard more than its customers did.

quiz.question: What did BlackBerry's CEO famously misjudge?
options: That consumers would prefer touchscreens over physical keyboards

details.summary: BlackBerry dominated business smartphones with its physical keyboard and secure email. When iPhone proved that consumers wanted touchscreens and apps, BlackBerry's CEO dismissed it, saying no one would trade a keyboard for a touchscreen..
details.whyItMatters: BlackBerry's failure illustrates how customer feedback from existing users can be dangerously misleading. Current customers loved the keyboard; future customers wanted the touchscreen. Listening to the wrong audience accelerated BlackBerry's decline.
takeaways: BlackBerry dominated business smartphones with physical keyboards and secure email
CEO dismissed the touchscreen iPhone as irrelevant to its core business users
Market share collapsed from 20 percent to under 1 percent in five years

faq.question: Why did BlackBerry's physical keyboard become a liability?
faq.answer: The physical keyboard consumed half the device's front face, limiting screen size. Touch keyboards freed the entire surface for display, enabling video, web browsing, and apps that the small BlackBerry screen could not support. The keyboard advantage became a screen disadvantage.

faq.question: What ultimately killed BlackBerry's phone business?
faq.answer: The app ecosystem gap. Developers built apps for iPhone and Android, not BlackBerry. Without apps, consumers chose competitors. Without consumers, developers had no incentive to build BlackBerry apps. This negative cycle drained the platform of both users and software.
